entities.summary:
Gilbert de la Porrée, also known as Gilbert of Poitiers, Gilbertus Porretanus or Pictaviensis, was a scholastic logician and theologian who played a crucial role in shaping the intellectual landscape of Western Europe during the 12th century.

Born in 1070 in Poitiers, France, de la Porrée rose to prominence as a professor of philosophy and theology at the University of Paris, where he taught alongside notable figures such as Thomas Becket and Peter Abelard.

De la Porrée's most significant contributions were in the fields of logic and theology, where he developed and systematized various concepts that would influence Western thought for centuries to come.

One of his most notable works, the 'Liber Poenitentiae', a treatise on penance and indulgences, was widely disseminated throughout Europe and played a significant role in shaping Catholic doctrine.

De la Porrée's legacy extends beyond his own work, as he contributed to the development of the University of Paris, which became a hub for intellectual inquiry and debate.

He died on September 11, 1154, leaving behind a legacy that continues to be studied and debated by scholars today.

Gilbert de la Porrée's significance can be seen in the numerous universities and institutions he helped establish, as well as his contributions to the development of scholasticism and the Catholic Church's doctrine on indulgences.

De la Porrée's work continues to be relevant in the 21st century, as scholars continue to grapple with the complexities of Catholic doctrine and the role of universities in shaping intellectual thought.

In the 21st century, de la Porrée's work continues to influence contemporary debates on Catholicism, scholasticism, and the role of universities in shaping intellectual thought.
